You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-10.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement

Current approaches in Neural Combinatorial Optimization (NCO) suffer from extreme specialization. While machine learning heuristics have achieved impressive results on specific tasks (such as the Traveling Salesman Problem), these models are typically "siloed": a model trained on one problem cannot solve another, and even slight variations in problem constraints often necessitate re-training from scratch. Unlike Natural Language Processing or Computer Vision, where foundation models generalize across tasks, CO lacks a unified architecture capable of handling the structural diversity of optimization problems (e.g., varying node types, edge attributes, and graph topologies). Consequently, the field is fragmented, requiring significant computational resources to train separate models for every new application.

## Core Hypothesis

We hypothesize that it is possible to construct a single, generalist "backbone" agent capable of solving a wide variety of combinatorial optimization problems by decoupling the problem-specific input/output formatting from the core reasoning logic.

Our intuition is that while surface-level constraints differ, the underlying heuristics required to solve routing, scheduling, and graph problems share algorithmic commonalities. By designing a flexible attention mechanism that natively integrates edge features and heterogeneous node types, and by training this backbone in a multi-task setting, we believe the model can learn a "meta-heuristic" that generalizes well to unseen problems with minimal fine-tuning.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)

We propose to design a unified architecture composed of a shared central backbone and lightweight, problem-specific adapters. Our approach focuses on three key architectural innovations to handle the discrepancy between different optimization tasks:

**1. Modular Input/Output via Shared Codebooks**
To bridge the gap between diverse problem definitions and a shared latent space, we will employ task-specific linear adapters. These adapters will project problem-specific features (nodes and edges) into a low-dimensional space. To ensure that different tasks map to compatible representations within the backbone—rather than occupying disjoint subspaces—we will enforce a bottleneck using a shared **codebook**. This codebook will project the low-dimensional task features into the high-dimensional embedding space of the backbone, effectively forcing the model to learn a common vocabulary across different problems.

**2. Mixed-Attention Mechanism**
Standard Transformers process node features well but often struggle to naturally incorporate edge-level information (which is critical in CO, representing distances, costs, or constraints). We propose a **Mixed-Attention** block. Instead of using positional encodings or graph biases, we will inject edge information directly into the core of the attention mechanism. Intuitively, the affinity score between two nodes will be computed by combining node-to-node interactions with edge-specific queries and keys. This allows the model to dynamically weigh the importance of relationships based on edge attributes (e.g., "is there a precedence constraint?") without altering the fundamental transformer architecture.

**3. Multi-Type Transformer Architecture**
Many CO problems (like scheduling) involve heterogeneous entities (e.g., "Jobs" vs. "Machines") that form multipartite graphs. Treating these simply as "nodes" loses semantic clarity. We propose a **Multi-Type** architecture where the attention blocks are duplicated to handle specific relationships (e.g., Job-to-Job, Job-to-Machine). Crucially, to maintain the "generalist" nature of the model, these duplicated blocks will **share the same parameters**. This allows the backbone to process complex, multi-modal graph structures using a single set of weights, dynamically adapting the computation path based on the node types present in the current task.

**Training Strategy**
We will train this model in a multi-task setting using Imitation Learning. We will generate expert trajectories from diverse problem classes (routing, scheduling, packing) using classical solvers. The model will learn to construct solutions sequentially, effectively treating optimization as a trajectory generation task.

## Expected Contribution

If successful, this project will deliver the first truly generalist neural solver for combinatorial optimization. Theoretically, it will demonstrate that CO heuristics are transferable across structurally distinct graph problems, challenging the prevailing assumption that NCO requires specialized architectures. Practically, this will enable a "foundation model" workflow for Operations Research: users will be able to solve novel problems by simply training lightweight adapters or fine-tuning the backbone on a handful of examples (few-shot learning), drastically reducing the time and data required to deploy neural heuristics in real-world scenarios.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We established a comprehensive experimental framework to evaluate the performance of a Generalist Combinatorial Optimization Agent Learner (GOAL). The setup was designed to assess the model's ability to handle multi-task learning across diverse problem types, zero-shot generalization to larger instances, and transfer learning (fine-tuning) to completely new problems.

*   **Training Tasks (8 Problems):** We selected eight classic combinatorial optimization problems spanning multiple domains:
    *   **Routing:** Asymmetric Traveling Salesman Problem (ATSP), Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (CVRP), Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem with Time Windows (CVRPTW), Orienteering Problem (OP).
    *   **Scheduling:** Job Shop Scheduling Problem (JSSP), Unrelated Machine Scheduling Problem (UMSP).
    *   **Packing:** Knapsack Problem (KP).
    *   **Graph:** Minimum Vertex Covering Problem (MVC).

*   **Transfer/Fine-Tuning Tasks (8 New Problems):** We utilized eight distinct problems unseen during training:
    *   Traveling Repairman Problem (TRP)
    *   Prize Collecting TSP (PCTSP)
    *   Open CVRP (OCVRP)
    *   Split Delivery CVRP (SDCVRP)
    *   Sequential Ordering Problem (SOP)
    *   Maximum Covering Location Problem (MCLP)
    *   Maximum Independent Set (MIS)
    *   Open Shop Scheduling Problem (OSSP)

*   **Datasets:**
    *   **Training Data:** We generated 1 million random instances for each of the 8 training tasks.
    *   **Instance Sizes:** Standard training size was 100 nodes for most problems. JSSP was $10 \times 10$ (100 operations), and UMSP was $100 \times 20$ (100 operations).
    *   **Validation/Test Data:** 128 instances per problem.
    *   **Generalization Data:** Instances of sizes 200, 500, and 1000 (and corresponding JSSP sizes $10 \times 15$, $15 \times 15$, $20 \times 15$) were generated to test scalability.

*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **Optimality Gap (%):** The relative gap between the model's solution and the solution provided by a task-specific oracle solver.
    *   **Computation Time:** Wall-clock time required to solve the test set (typically 128 instances).

*   **Baselines Compared:**
    *   **Neural Constructive Models:** AM, MDAM, POMO (no augmentation), Sym-NCO, BQ-NCO, MVMoE/4E, RouteFinder-TE, MatNet, S2V-DQN, COMPASS, Gumbeldore.
    *   **Oracle Solvers:** LKH (ATSP, CVRP, SOP, TRP), HGS (CVRPTW), A4OP (OP), ORTools (KP, JSSP, PCTSP, UMSP), FastWVC (MVC), PuLP2 (MCLP), Concorde (Euclidean TSP).

*   **Implementation Details:**
    *   **Model Architecture:** 9-layer backbone, embedding size 128, feed-forward dimension 512, 8 attention heads, ReZero normalization.
    *   **Adapters:** Task-specific input adapters projected features to low dimensions (nodes: 8, edges: 4) before mapping to the backbone via a shared codebook.
    *   **Optimizer:** AdamW.
    *   **Learning Rate:** Initial rate of 0.0005, decay rate of 0.97 every 10th epoch.
    *   **Loss Functions:** Single-class cross-entropy (ATSP, CVRP, CVRPTW, OP, JSSP, UMSP); Multi-class cross-entropy (KP, MVC).
    *   **Training Hardware:** 8 Nvidia V100 GPU servers.
    *   **Batch Size:** 256.
    *   **Duration:** Approximately 7 days (ca. 400 epochs).
    *   **Decoding Strategy:** Greedy decoding was used for all reported results to ensure fair comparison.

## 3. Qualitative Observations

We derived the following observations from the visual data and textual analysis of the experiments:

**Model Architecture and Versatility**
*   **Single-Task Performance:** We observed that when trained as a specialized single-task model, GOAL achieved the best performance (lowest optimality gap) in 7 out of the 8 training tasks compared to baselines.
*   **Multi-Task Performance:** The multi-task version of GOAL, using a single shared backbone, performed only slightly worse than the specialized single-task versions. This confirmed that the backbone effectively shared parameters across diverse tasks.
*   **Structural Handling:** The architecture successfully handled single-type problems (using standard mixed-attention) and multi-type problems (using duplicated mixed-attention blocks with shared parameters) within the same framework.

**Fine-Tuning and Transfer Learning**
*   **Unsupervised Fine-Tuning Efficiency:** When fine-tuning on 8 new unseen tasks (TRP, PCTSP, OCVRP, SDCVRP, SOP, MCLP, MIS, OSSP) using an unsupervised imitation-improvement strategy, GOAL consistently outperformed training a model from scratch given a comparable time budget (up to 5.5 hours).
*   **Supervised Fine-Tuning Efficiency:** We observed that supervised fine-tuning using only 128 labeled instances and limited training steps allowed the model to reach low optimality gaps (e.g., 0.92% on TRP, 0.11% on SOP) in a matter of minutes (typically under 3.5 minutes).
*   **Synergistic Transfer:** When comparing fine-tuning of the multi-task GOAL versus fine-tuning single-task models on new problems, the multi-task model consistently performed as well as or better than the most structurally similar single-task model (e.g., the CVRP-specialized model applied to OCVRP). This suggests the multi-task training induced a synergistic effect beneficial for transfer.

**Ablation Studies**
*   **Mixed-Attention Mechanism:** On the ATSP task, we observed that our proposed mixed-attention blocks significantly outperformed alternative edge-mixing mechanisms (MatNet and G2G) in terms of both final optimality gap and convergence speed.
*   **Multi-Type Architecture:** For the Job Shop Scheduling Problem (JSSP), which involves heterogeneous node types, the proposed multi-type architecture converged faster and achieved a significantly lower optimality gap (4.6%) compared to a single-type model that simply stacked features (8.9%).
*   **Codebook Impact:** While the shared codebook (used to sparsify input adapters) did not significantly impact performance on training tasks, it was crucial for fine-tuning. We observed that models with the codebook exhibited more stable fine-tuning trajectories and achieved better final optimality gaps across the transfer tasks compared to models without the codebook.

**Generalization Capabilities**
*   **Zero-Shot Scaling:** We observed strong zero-shot generalization to instances up to 10 times larger than the training set. Specifically for ATSP, GOAL maintained a low optimality gap (1.96% on 1000 nodes) whereas baselines like BQ-NCO degraded significantly (8.09%).

Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs

• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.

Conference Guidelines
# ICLR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the LaTeX paper writing process for ICLR 2025.

## General Setup
* **Document Class:** `\documentclass{article}`
* **Required Packages:**
    ```latex
    \usepackage{iclr2025_conference,times}
    \usepackage{hyperref}
    \usepackage{url}
    % Optional but recommended for math
    \input{math_commands.tex}
    ```
* **Style Files:** You must use `iclr2025_conference.sty` and `iclr2025_conference.bst`.

## Anonymity (Crucial)
* ICLR is double-blind. **Do not** include real author names or affiliations in the submission version, use "Ambitious AI Researcher" instead.
* Use the third person when citing your own prior work (e.g., "Earlier work by Smalle (2024)..." instead of "In our earlier work...").
* You may post your paper on arXiv, but do not explicitly refer to the arXiv version in the paper to maintain anonymity.

## Paper Length
* **Main Text:** Strict upper limit of **10 pages**.
* **Citations:** Unlimited additional pages.
* **Ethics & Reproducibility Statements:** Optional. Do not count toward the page limit (max 1 page each).
* **Acknowledgments:** Do not count toward the page limit.

## Abstract
The abstract must be limited to **one paragraph**.
* **Margins:** Indented 1/2 inch (3 picas) on both left and right-hand margins.
* **Font:** 10-point type, vertical spacing of 11-points.
* **Title:** The word `\textsc{Abstract}` must be centered, in small caps, and in point size 12.
* **Spacing:** Two line spaces precede the abstract.

## Formatting Your Paper
The text must be confined within a rectangle 5.5 inches (33 picas) wide and 9 inches (54 picas) long. The left margin is 1.5 inch (9 picas).
* **Font:** Times New Roman (via `times` package) is preferred.
* **Size:** 10-point type with 11-point vertical spacing.
* **Paragraphs:** Separated by 1/2 line space, with **no indentation**.
* **Paper Title:** 17-point, small caps, left-aligned.

### Headings
* **First Level:** Small caps (`\textsc`), flush left, 12-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.
* **Second Level:** Small caps, flush left, 10-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.
* **Third Level:** Small caps, flush left, 10-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.

## Citations and References
Use the `natbib` package (loaded automatically by the style file).
* **Narrative citation:** Use `\citet{Gomu2024}` $\rightarrow$ "Gomu et al. (2024)".
* **Parenthetical citation:** Use `\citep{Gomu2024}` $\rightarrow$ "(Gomu et al., 2024)".
* **Bibliography:**
    ```latex
    \bibliography{references}
    \bibliographystyle{iclr2025_conference}
    ```

## Figures and Tables
* All artwork must be neat, clean, and legible.
* **Captions:** Lower case (except for first word and proper nouns).
* **Placement:**
    * **Figures:** Caption appears **after** (below) the figure.
    * **Tables:** Caption appears **before** (above) the table.

## Math Notation
* ICLR encourages standardized notation using `\input{math_commands.tex}` (based on the Deep Learning book notation).
* Variables: Italics ($a$, $\va$, $\mA$).
* Random Variables: Roman ($P(\ra)$).
* Sets: Blackboard bold ($\R$, $\sA$).
* Functions: Standard LaTeX ($f(\vx)$).

## Optional Statements
These should appear at the end of the main text, before references.
1.  **Ethics Statement:** (Optional, max 1 page) Address potential concerns (human subjects, sensitive data, bias, etc.).
2.  **Reproducibility Statement:** (Optional, max 1 page) Reference code, proofs, or data processing steps to ensure reproducibility.

references.text:
## Problem Statement

The field of Neural Combinatorial Optimization (NCO) currently suffers from extreme fragmentation. While constructive neural heuristics have achieved success in specific domains (e.g., Vehicle Routing, TSP), these models are strictly specialized. A model trained for the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) cannot solve a Vehicle Routing Problem (CVRP), nor can it handle slight variations in problem constraints without re-training from scratch.

Unlike Natural Language Processing or Computer Vision, where foundation models leverage intrinsic regularities in data (text or pixels), Combinatorial Optimization (CO) problems are defined on graphs with highly variable structures. There is currently no mechanism to handle the discrepancies between problems that rely purely on node features, those heavily dependent on edge attributes (distances, costs), and those defined on multipartite graphs (scheduling). The lack of a unified representation prevents the development of a "Generalist" agent capable of transfer learning or solving multi-task distributions.

## Core Hypothesis

We hypothesize that we can construct a **Generalist Combinatorial Optimization Agent Learner (GOAL)** by decoupling problem-specific feature extraction from a shared, problem-agnostic reasoning backbone.

Our core technical hypothesis is that a single transformer-based backbone can learn to solve arbitrary tail-recursive CO problems if we introduce two specific architectural innovations:
1.  **Mixed-Attention Mechanism:** A modified attention block that injects edge-specific information directly into the query-key scalar products, allowing the model to process problems with arbitrary combinations of node and edge features seamlessly.
2.  **Multi-Type Weight Sharing:** A strategy for handling heterogeneous graph structures (e.g., bipartite graphs in scheduling) by dynamically instantiating self-attention and cross-attention blocks that share a single set of parameters.

We predict that by projecting task-specific inputs into a shared embedding space via a **low-rank codebook**, the backbone will learn generalized algorithmic policies that can be fine-tuned to new, unseen NP-hard problems with minimal data.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will formulate the solution as a constructive sequential decision-making process. We will define the multi-task environment as a disjoint union of Bisimulation Quotient MDPs (BQ-MDPs), where states correspond to problem instances and actions correspond to construction steps (node selections).

### 1. Task Representation and Input Adapters
For any given task $t$, we define an instance as a tuple $(x, \bar{x})$, where:
*   $x \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times F_t}$ represents the feature vectors of $N$ nodes (dimension $F_t$).
*   $\bar{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N \times \bar{F}_t}$ represents the feature vectors of edges (dimension $\bar{F}_t$).

To map these variable dimensions to a shared backbone embedding dimension $D$, we will employ **Task-Specific Adapters** combined with a **Shared Codebook**.
Rather than a direct linear projection, which risks subspace specialization, we will enforce low-rank projections.
1.  **Input Adapter:** A task-specific linear layer maps inputs to a low dimension $\ell \ll D$.
2.  **Shared Codebook:** A learnable matrix of size $\ell \times D$ projects this compressed representation into the backbone space.

### 2. Backbone Architecture: Mixed-Attention
The core of our architecture will be a Transformer stack (proposed depth $L=9$, embedding $D=128$) utilizing a novel **Multi-Head Mixed-Attention** mechanism. Unlike standard positional encoding, this mechanism ingests edge features $\bar{x}$ directly into the attention score computation.

For a given head $h$, let $M$ be the number of query nodes and $N$ be the number of key/value nodes. We define the projections for queries ($Q$), keys ($K$), and values ($V$) as:
$$ Q_n^{(h)} = Q_n \mathbf{W}_Q^{(h)}, \quad K_m^{(h)} = K_m \mathbf{W}_K^{(h)}, \quad V_m^{(h)} = V_m \mathbf{W}_V^{(h)} $$

Simultaneously, we define projections for the edge features $E_{mn}$ (derived from $\bar{x}$):
$$ Q_{mn}^{\prime (h)} = E_{mn} \mathbf{W}_Q^{\prime (h)}, \quad K_{mn}^{\prime (h)} = E_{mn} \mathbf{W}_K^{\prime (h)} $$

The attention scores $S_{mn}^{(h)}$ will be computed by adding the edge-derived vectors to the node-derived vectors *before* the scalar product:
$$ S_{mn}^{(h)} = \langle K_m^{(h)} + K_{mn}^{\prime (h)} \mid Q_n^{(h)} + Q_{mn}^{\prime (h)} \rangle $$

This formulation allows the model to structurally integrate relational data (distances, precedence constraints) without computational overhead when such features are absent (in which case the edge terms are zero).

### 3. Multi-Type Transformer for Heterogeneous Graphs
To handle problems with heterogeneous node types (e.g., "Jobs" vs. "Machines" in Scheduling), we will implement a **Multi-Type Architecture**.

Instead of padding disparate types into a single tensor, we will dynamically compose the layer operations based on the task structure:
*   **Node Processing:** We will instantiate separate self-attention blocks for each node type.
*   **Edge Processing:** We will instantiate cross-attention blocks for valid type pairings.
*   **Parameter Sharing:** Crucially, all attention blocks within a specific layer will share the **exact same parameters** ($\mathbf{W}_Q, \mathbf{W}_K, \mathbf{W}_V, \text{etc.}$), regardless of whether they are performing self-attention or cross-attention.

### 4. Training Protocol
We will train the model in a multi-task setting via **Imitation Learning**.
*   **Objective:** We will minimize the cross-entropy loss between the model's predicted action probabilities (softmax over valid nodes) and the decisions made by expert oracles (e.g., LKH for routing, CP-SAT for scheduling).
*   **Output Adapter:** A task-specific linear projection will map the backbone output to a score matrix $y \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times K_t}$, representing the log-logits for selecting specific nodes.

## Expected Contribution

1.  **Unified Architecture:** We expect to provide the first neural architecture capable of ingesting arbitrary CO problems (Routing, Scheduling, Packing) regardless of their graph structure (simple vs. multipartite) or feature density (node-heavy vs. edge-heavy).
2.  **State-of-the-Art Multi-Tasking:** We anticipate that a single trained backbone will perform competitively with specialized single-task models, validating the existence of shared algorithmic reasoning across different NP-hard problems.
3.  **Foundation for Transfer Learning:** The proposed architecture intends to enable rapid fine-tuning on unseen problems. By freezing the backbone and training only the light-weight adapters (or fine-tuning the whole model with limited data), we expect to achieve high-quality solutions on new tasks orders of magnitude faster than training from scratch.

network.web_access: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.

preinstalled.zh: 编排镜像：上游代码（固定提交、未改）、uv 锁定依赖、docker CLI（经 shim 给兄弟容器加代理和 CA）；agent 镜像：上游自己的 agent-cli Dockerfile
preinstalled.en: orchestrator image: upstream code at the pin (unmodified), uv-locked dependencies, the docker CLI (a shim adds proxy and CA to sibling containers); agent image: upstream's own agent-cli Dockerfile

notes.benchmark_paths: A benchmark item's paths are mounted into the agent containers unless upstream mounts the same path itself (/workspace and below, /home/agent-home, /task-source, /run, /tmp): those are left out and listed in logs/sibling-mounts.txt. The agents work in upstream's own /workspace (the run directory), so a deliverable the official prompt names under such a path is not written where the run collects it.
notes.venue: paper.paper_format=iclr for every task. The system has only iclr and alife specs and does not choose a venue itself; ICML and NeurIPS templates and a system-chosen venue are unsupported.
notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. The paradigm is optimisation of a scalar score: the task-drafting phase (documented as experimental) turns the brief into an evaluator and a seed program.
notes.phases: execution.phases=task_drafting,investigation,final_evaluation,paper; the system's own default also runs ablations and posthoc; final_evaluation stays because a drafted task requires it before the paper. review/revision (second model) are never selected.

preinstalled.zh: python:3.11 bookworm；上游代码按 PYTHONPATH 使用；pdflatex + bibtex；CPU 版 PyTorch 和 numpy、scipy、scikit-learn、pandas、matplotlib 等（constraints.txt 固定）
preinstalled.en: python:3.11 bookworm; upstream code via PYTHONPATH; pdflatex + bibtex; CPU PyTorch with numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib and more (pinned by constraints.txt)

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

agent.how: no external coding agent: EvoScientist's in-process sub-agents (LangChain deepagents)

tools.permissions: think_tool, deepagents built-ins, EvoSkills skills and an execute shell; skill_manager not registered; no search tool

preinstalled.zh: 上游锁定依赖（uv sync --frozen）加兼容补丁 compat.patch；TeX Live（含 fonts-extra、latexmk）；给 agent 用的研究 Python 环境 /opt/research
preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
